extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent owners/clients, and counsel preparing for Markman (claim construction) proceedings in U.S. courts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on preparing for and conducting a Markman (claim construction) hearing in U.S. district court, describing evidence types, timing and formats, governing rules (Phillips/37 CFR 42.100), and practical preparatory tasks and deliverables (claim charts, tutorials, expert support).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a Markman hearing (Claim Construction Hearing)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markman hearing is a pre-trial hearing in a U.S. District Court during which a judge examines evidence from all parties on the appropriate meanings of relevant keywords used in a patent claim when patent infringement is alleged by a plaintiff. It is also known as a 'Claim Construction Hearing'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This hearing is focused on construing claim language (what is and is not protected). The judge, not the jury, determines the meaning of claim terms for the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of claim construction for infringement outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the patent claims specify what constitutes and does not constitute protected intellectual property, claim construction is crucial in resolving patent disputes; the court determines patent infringement cases by interpreting the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A favorable claim construction ruling can indicate likely case outcomes and often encourages settlement. The judge’s claim construction finding informs jury instructions and the jury then determines whether infringement occurred (including application of the doctrine of equivalents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge vs. jury roles in patent trials
rubrics_metrics.description: The judge decides how claims should be understood (claim construction) while the jury is the fact-finder that decides whether infringement actually occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the Seventh Amendment protects the right to a jury trial, the Supreme Court (Markman) held that judges, experienced in interpreting written language, are better suited to define claim terms. The jury’s infringement decision must be informed by the judge’s claim construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic evidence to be used in claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Materials provided as a part of the patent application are referred to as intrinsic evidence. This comprises the claims, executive summary, and written description contained in the patent application itself, written or verbal correspondence between the patent applicant and the patent examiner that includes the prosecution history, prior art cited in the patent application, and previous comparable patents and their prosecution histories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts generally look at intrinsic evidence as primary authority when construing claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extrinsic evidence and its proper role
rubrics_metrics.description: Any evidence that originates from outside sources is considered extrinsic. Extrinsic evidence in Markman hearings may include: definitions from dictionaries for common terms, for technical words consult encyclopedias or engineering dictionaries, journals, or other scholarly works that cover the technology, the patent applicant’s testimony, or expert opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extrinsic evidence is helpful for education and background knowledge on the contested invention, but courts generally treat it as secondary to intrinsic evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governing claim construction approach (Phillips v. AWH Corp.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phillips v. AWH Corp. (Federal Circuit, 2004) established the current method for construing patent claims. The correct claim construction cannot be determined using a predetermined process; instead, a set of criteria are applied to choose the right construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Later decisions have cited Phillips as foundational. The Phillips framework emphasizes intrinsic evidence, considers extrinsic evidence cautiously, and rejects rigid, single-step rules for construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO alignment for PTAB proceedings (37 CFR 42.100)
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.S. Patent Office finalized a regulation to align its claim construction guidelines with the Federal Circuit’s Phillips ruling. The Patent Office will interpret patent claims for inter partes review (IPR), post-grant review (PGR), and covered business method patents (CBM) procedures in accordance with this rule, as outlined in 37 CFR 42.100.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This regulation applies to petitions submitted after it was adopted and is relevant when preparing claim construction contentions for USPTO post-grant proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court discretion on whether to hold a Markman hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: The district court has the discretion to determine whether a Markman hearing is required. A Markman hearing is not mandatory simply because of the Markman v. Westview Instruments ruling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many district judges decline a live Markman hearing where the paper record provides sufficient detail. Whether to hold a hearing depends on the particulars of the case and the court’s procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and procedural variations of Markman hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markman hearing is often scheduled at an advanced stage of the trial, but procedures vary: some districts reach early construction decisions before addressing infringement, others wait until after all evidence is heard and then give jury instructions at the end of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hearing formats vary (paper-only submissions, multi-day live hearings with witnesses). Some courts allow experts to testify in ways that limit questioning; practices vary by district and judge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred hearing formats and practical considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Many lawyers and judges prefer the paper-only format to a multi-day live hearing with numerous witnesses. Some courts will permit specialists to testify without being questioned themselves or by outside witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should consider the district’s local practices and whether technical tutorials, charts, or live expert testimony will most effectively communicate disputed claim meanings to the judge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantiating claim construction through documentation and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantiate claim construction through critical review of specification, prosecution history, and expert evidence; draft opinions, notes, and documentation required to substantiate the scope/interpretation of claims and/or claim terms/elements and limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare detailed claim charts, mapping sheets, and technical analyses that align claim language to specification disclosures and prosecution history to justify proposed constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing expert credibility and preparing expert materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish credibility and credentials of the testifying expert; provide technical tutorials and charts to help judges understand the claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IIPRD-style support includes preparing technical tutorials, expert support for depositions, help with document requests, requests for admission, interrogatories, and other materials to build effective expert testimony and background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using claim charts to set up validity defenses and map prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Set up a validity defence through comprehensive claim charts demonstrating scope of each claim term/element/limitation and mapping with prior art reference(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed claim charts help both invalidity and non-infringement strategies by showing where prior art reads on claimed limitations or where accused products fall outside claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing claim construction contentions in compliance with USPTO guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare patent claim construction contentions in compliance with claim construction guidelines established by the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure contentions conform to PTAB/USPTO procedural rules for IPR/PGR/CBM petitions (including timing and form requirements) to avoid procedural rejection or sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical support activities for Markman proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide assistance in preparing formal documents, technical disclosures, mapping sheets, deposition support, preparing document requests, preparing requests for admission, interrogatories, and other discovery-related activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehensive pre-hearing preparation and supporting materials can simplify complex technical claims for the court and strengthen claim construction positions.
